---
title: Architecture
---

This section explains how Starsim 4 is put together and why. It is for two kinds of reader: a modeler who wants to know what happens when they call `sim.run()`, and a prospective contributor deciding whether this is a codebase they could work in. You don't need any of it to use Starsim; the [user guide](../user_guide/intro_starsim.qmd) is the place for that.

## The idea in one paragraph

A model in Starsim 4 is written once, as data: states (`S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')`), transitions between them (`S >> I @ beta * I`), and parameters, with the mixing, demography and interventions around them. Each disease checks its own structure when it is made (unknown names, rates of the wrong shape). When the sim is initialized, Starsim reads those objects, fills in what was left out (and records each guess), checks them against each other, and chooses how to run them: as a deterministic ODE, as one of three stochastic compartmental solvers, or as agents. Because the model is data rather than code, everything else is derived from the same objects: the printed description, the equations, the diagram, the hash that identifies a run, the saved model spec, the code that rebuilds it, and the exports to other frameworks. One declared model, several ways to run it, and one source of truth for all of them.

Models written the Starsim 3 way, as classes with their own `step()` code, still work: they run as agents through the same loop, and can sit beside declared models in one sim.

## The principles behind it

Every design choice is checked against a short constitution. In order of weight:

- **Simplicity.** Writing and changing a model should be easy for an epidemiologist, not just an engineer. A model ported to Starsim should get shorter.
- **Performance.** As close to custom compiled code as is feasible. This is why compartmental runs go through compiled kernels and why agents use compiled passes over their arrays.
- **Flexibility.** Every major modeling feature should be expressible, even if not every one is built in. When a declaration can't say something, a module's `step()` can.
- **Correctness.** The machinery is validated by tests, but over-correctness should not cost simplicity or speed: Euler steps, Erlang stages and other standard approximations are fine, as long as they are announced.

After these come understandability (few concepts, no brittle subsystems), maintainability (solvers should not each reimplement the same thing), composability (use as much or as little of Starsim as you want), short startup (no long compilation before a small run), and being easy for AI tools to work with. The development principles add: no legacy shims, avoid bloat, and think about the whole system before adding a special path for one case.

You'll see these principles in specific choices throughout this section. For example, `solver='auto'` picks the simplest representation that runs the model faithfully (simplicity, performance); every approximation prints one line saying what was done (correctness without refusing); and the compiled kernels are optional (short startup).

## The map

Starsim has five layers. Broadly, each builds on the ones before it, and a contributor can usually work in one layer at a time.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart TD
    D["<b>1. Declaration</b><br/>states, transitions, rates,<br/>parameters, dimensions"]
    G["<b>The graph</b><br/>resolved, completed, checked"]
    O["<b>2. Build and orchestration</b><br/>sim.init(), the loop, modules,<br/>people, networks, results"]
    C{"choose a solver"}
    K["<b>3. Compartmental engine</b><br/>ode, binomial, gillespie, tau"]
    A["<b>3. Agent engine</b><br/>abm"]
    J["<b>4. Speed and alternate backends</b><br/>Numba kernels, JAX, compiled draws"]
    E["<b>5. Edges</b><br/>fitting, model spec, interop,<br/>library, geography"]
    D --> G --> O --> C
    C --> K
    C --> A
    K -.-> J
    A -.-> J
    O --- E
```

| Layer | Files in `starsim/` | What they do |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Declaration | `transitions.py`, `expressions.py`, `parameters.py`, `distributions.py`, `time.py`, `dates.py`, `conditions.py`, `dimensions.py`, `strains.py`, `graph.py` | The words a model is written in: states and transitions, rates as expressions (`beta * I`), parameters (`ss.par`, `ss.by`), durations and rates with units, conditions for `where=`, stratifications and strains. `graph.py` collects one module's declarations into an `ss.transitions.Graph`, names them, fills in defaults (recording each guess), and checks them. |
| 2. Build and orchestration | `sim.py`, `loop.py`, `timeline.py`, `modules.py`, `people.py`, `arrays.py`, `networks.py`, `diseases.py`, `demographics.py`, `pregnancy.py`, `interventions.py`, `products.py`, `connectors.py`, `analyzers.py`, `results.py`, `run.py` | The runtime objects. `sim.init()` builds the population, the modules and the results, and chooses the solver; the loop then calls each module in a fixed, printable order each step. `ss.Module` is the one base class for diseases, networks, demographics, interventions, connectors and analyzers. `run.py` runs many sims (`ss.MultiSim`, `ss.parallel`). |
| 3. Engines | `solvers/choose.py`, `solvers/engine.py`, `solvers/compartmental.py`, `solvers/mixing.py`, `solvers/agents.py`, `solvers/crossing.py`, `solvers/deliveries.py`, `solvers/particles.py`, `kernels.py` | How a graph is run. `choose.py` picks the solver and says why. Each declared module gets one engine: `Compartmental` (which flattens the model into a program of flows that the Numba kernels in `kernels.py` step) or `Agents` (boolean arrays over agents). `crossing.py` tracks several diseases jointly when one refers to another's states. |
| 4. Speed and alternate backends | `gradients.py`, `perflib/` (`_chain.py`, `_draws.py`, `_passes.py`, `_jit.py`, `_memory.py`, `_cache.py`) | The same runs, faster or differentiable. `gradients.py` runs the ODE in JAX for gradients and many runs at once; `_chain.py` runs the chain binomial and tau-leaping in JAX; `_draws.py` has the exact random draws the kernels share; `_passes.py` the compiled passes over agents and network edges; `_jit.py` is `ss.jit`, for compiling users' own code. No user needs to read these. |
| 5. Edges | `fit.py`, `spec.py`, `presentation.py`, `errors.py`, `geo.py`, `data.py`, `interop/`, `library/` | What builds on a run model. Fitting (`sim.fit()`); the model spec, hashes and `to_code()`; `describe()`, `diagram()` and `equations()`; the catalog of errors and notes; places, mobility and data by place name; importers and exporters for other frameworks; and example diseases and networks (`import starsim.library as ssl`). |

Helpers that every layer uses are in `settings.py` (`ss.options`), `utils.py`, `debugtools.py` and `timeplot.py`.

For a sense of scale, the package is about 69,000 lines of Python: about 13,000 in declaration, 19,000 in orchestration, 13,000 in the engines and kernels, 7,000 in the speed layer, and 15,000 at the edges (half of that in `interop/`). The core that a model passes through on every run is layers 1 to 3.

A few things to notice in the map:

- **A declaration doesn't say how it will run.** The states, transitions and parameters of layer 1 are the same objects whether the model runs as an ODE or as agents; only when they are evaluated (a rate, a condition) do they see one value per group or one per agent. That is what makes the solver a choice rather than part of the model.
- **Every compartmental solver steps the same program.** The ODE, the chain binomial, Gillespie and tau-leaping all run the flat list of flows that `Compartmental` builds. The JAX backends and the particle filter run that same program too, so a fix in one place is a fix for all of them.
- **Code is never analyzed in advance.** A function in a rate, or a module's `step()`, is simply called with what the solver has (one value per agent, or one per group). If it asks for something that only agents have, the run stops and says so.

## The pages in this section

- [The model as data](model.qmd): states, transitions, rates and parameters as objects, and how the graph resolves, completes and checks them.
- [From model to run](build_and_run.qmd): what `sim.init()` does, units and time, and the order modules run in each step.
- [Solvers](solvers.qmd): how the solver is chosen, the engines that run each one, and how approximations are announced.
- [Mixing, interventions, and results](interactions.qmd): networks and mixing pools, `ss.modify`, deliveries, and results.
- [Randomness and fitting](randomness_and_fitting.qmd): random streams and common random numbers, and how calibration chooses its method.
- [The model spec, errors, and interop](spec_and_interop.qmd): the JSON form of a model, the error catalog, and importers and exporters.
- [How the design is tested](testing.qmd): the test suites, what each guards, and which tests to run when you change something.
